content: Misoprostol is a prostaglandin that can be administered orally. Although it is not licensed for labor induction in most countries, it is widely used due to its affordability and stability under heat. The purpose of this review was to evaluate the effectiveness and safety of oral misoprostol for inducing labor in women with a viable fetus. A systematic search was conducted in the Cochrane Pregnancy and Childbirth Group's Trials Register as of January 17, 2014. Randomized controlled trials comparing oral misoprostol with placebo or other labor induction methods in women with a viable fetus were included. Data from these trials were independently assessed by two reviewers using standardized data collection forms. The review included 75 trials involving a total of 13,793 women. The quality of the trials varied. In nine trials comparing oral misoprostol with placebo (1,109 women), oral misoprostol significantly increased the likelihood of vaginal delivery within 24 hours (risk ratio [RR] 0.16, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.05 to 0.49; one trial; 96 women) and reduced the likelihood of cesarean delivery (RR 0.72, 95% CI 0.54 to 0.95; eight trials; 1,029 women). The risk of uterine hyperstimulation with fetal heart rate changes was not significantly different (RR 2.71, 95% CI 0.84 to 8.68; seven trials; 669 women). When oral misoprostol was compared with vaginal prostaglandin (dinoprostone) in 10 trials (3,240 women), there was little difference in the rates of vaginal delivery within 24 hours (RR 1.10, 95% CI 0.99 to 1.22; five trials; 2,128 women), uterine hyperstimulation with fetal heart rate changes (RR 0.95, 95% CI 0.59 to 1.53; seven trials; 2,352 women), and cesarean delivery (RR 0.92, 95% CI 0.81 to 1.04; 10 trials; 3,240 women). In five trials comparing oral misoprostol with intracervical prostaglandin E2 (681 women), oral misoprostol was associated with fewer failures to achieve vaginal delivery within 24 hours (RR 0.78, 95% CI 0.63 to 0.97; three trials; 452 women) but a higher incidence of uterine hyperstimulation with fetal heart rate changes (RR 3.57, 95% CI 1.11 to 11.54; three trials; 490 women). The data for this comparison were limited, and the differences in cesarean delivery rates were small (RR 0.85, 95% CI 0.63 to 1.16; five trials; 742 women). Nine trials compared oral misoprostol with intravenous oxytocin (1,282 women). There were no significant differences in the rates of vaginal delivery within 24 hours (RR 0.79, 95% CI 0.59 to 1.05; six trials; 789 women) or uterine hyperstimulation with fetal heart rate changes (RR 1.30, 95% CI 0.43 to 3.91; seven trials; 947 women). However, oral misoprostol was associated with fewer cesarean deliveries (RR 0.77, 95% CI 0.60 to 0.98; nine trials; 1,282 women). Thirty-seven trials compared oral misoprostol with vaginal misoprostol (6,417 women). There were no significant differences in the rates of vaginal delivery within 24 hours (RR 1.08, 95% CI 0.86 to 1.36; 14 trials; 2,448 women), uterine hyperstimulation with fetal heart rate changes (RR 0.71, 95% CI 0.47 to 1.08; 29 trials; 5,503 women), or cesarean delivery (RR 0.93, 95% CI 0.81 to 1.07; 35 trials; 6,326 women). Serious neonatal or maternal morbidity or mortality was rare, and no meaningful conclusions could be drawn regarding these outcomes. In conclusion, oral misoprostol is an effective agent for inducing labor and is more effective than placebo. It is as effective as vaginal misoprostol and vaginal dinoprostone and results in fewer cesarean deliveries compared to oxytocin alone. In settings where misoprostol is not licensed for labor induction, practitioners may prefer to use licensed alternatives such as dinoprostone. However, if oral misoprostol is used, evidence supports a dose of 20 to 25 mcg in solution. Oral regimens are generally safer than vaginal regimens, particularly in situations where there is a high risk of ascending infection or limited availability of staff for close monitoring.
